entries.title: Ryu Murakami, cult Japanese author, dies aged 74

entries.content:
Ryu Murakami, the cult Japanese author and film-maker whose subversive, blackly comic novels found millions of readers, has died aged 74. He died on 17 October at home, according to his Japanese publisher Gentosha.

Described as the enfant terrible of contemporary Japanese literature, Murakami incorporated violence, explicit drug use and sex into stories that offered a sharp-eyed critique of Japanese and American culture.

“It has been a huge privilege to bring many of Ryu Murakami’s strange, original and cinematic novels to an English-speaking audience,” said Adam Freudenheim, publisher and managing director at Pushkin Press, which, along with Bloomsbury, publishes Murakami’s works in translation in the UK.

Murakami was the son of two teachers, born in Sasebo, Nagasaki prefecture, in 1952. During high school, he joined a rock band as a drummer, and after participating in a rooftop protest was placed under a three-month house arrest. He published his first novel, Almost Transparent Blue, in 1976. The book, written while he was still a student, is narrated by a character called Ryū, and depicts the hedonistic lifestyle of a group of disillusioned, nihilistic young people. It won the Gunzo prize for new writers along with the Akutagawa prize, Japan’s most prestigious literary award.

Murakami was not related to his better-known namesake, Haruki. Ryu Murakami’s books are “edgier and angrier” wrote the journalist David Pilling in 2013. “If Haruki is the Beatles of Japanese literature, Ryu is its Rolling Stones”.

Murakami went on to write more than 40 novels and short story collections, including Coin Locker Babies, In the Miso Soup, Audition, Piercing and Popular Hits of the Showa Era. Most of his books have not yet been translated into English.

Many of his works have been adapted for screen, either by himself or other film-makers. The best-known is Audition, a 1999 feature film directed by Takashi Miike. The story follows a widower holding fake movie auditions in order to find a new girlfriend. Writing about the novel in the Guardian in 2009, Irvine Welsh described its prose as “elegiac and affecting, but it has the sharp, visceral feel of the butcher’s knife or surgeon’s scalpel”.

Murakami’s third novel, Coin Locker Babies, about children abandoned in storage lockers, won the Noma literary new face prize. The novel is “a surreal coming-of-age horror story that runs wildly through the heights of love and superstardom, and the lows of insanity and murder”, wrote Russell Thomas in the Guardian in 2020, selecting the novel as one of the best books set in Japan. “Murakami’s stories never shy away from shining a light on the darkest corners of society,” he added.

“All at Pushkin Press are saddened to hear of his death and extend our sympathies to his many readers around the world,” said Freudenheim.

entries.title: Lessons in Chemistry author Bonnie Garmus: ‘I wrote my first novel at 12 – it has not yet found a publisher’
entries.summary: The author of the global sensation on being inspired by Harper Lee, the craft of Joan Didion, and the joys of rereading Louisa May AlcottMy earliest reading memory I have a very clear memory of reading Fun With Dick and Jane. entries.content:
My earliest reading memory

I have a very clear memory of reading Fun With Dick and Jane. I was four years old, and my dad wrote each word on a chalkboard. I memorised them, then opened the book and read them back to him. I couldn’t believe it. It felt like magic! When I was older, I stumbled across the book and was surprised to find Dick and Jane didn’t really have all that much fun.

My favourite book growing up

Harriet the Spy by Louise Fitzhugh. Eleven-year-old Harriet Welch wants to be a writer, and her nanny encourages her to keepa notebook so she can practise writing every day. But when the other kids at school find her book (which is filled with her meanest, most vulnerable thoughts), she quickly becomes the school pariah. I must have read this story a hundred times. Harriet Welch was the reason I started writing stuff down. She was also the reason I understood that no matter how hard it feels, it is imperative to own and apologise for your mistakes.

The book that changed me as a teenager

To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee. Scout’s voice grabbed me from the start. It was a deep dive into racism, poverty, hatred and social justice, and it had a direct impact on how I saw the world.

The writer who changed my mind

Henry David Thoreau. “I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately,” he wrote in Walden, “to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.” I was 18, loved the outdoors, craved adventure, and desperately wanted to see what I was made of. But it’s hard to get work from a mountaintop, so I settled for living deliberately in my tiny, overpriced, noisy, too-hot apartment. Survival comes in many forms.

The book that made me want to be a writer

Fun With Dick and Jane! Seriously. I was in love with reading from the very beginning, and writing a story seemed like the obvious next step. At age five I wrote my first book. It was a page long and included an illustration. It has not yet been picked up by a publisher. I also wrote an entire novel by 12. For some reason, that, too, remains unsigned. All offers considered.

The book I came back to

Little Women by Louisa May Alcott. I was supposed to love it (I was nine; I fitted the demographic), but it didn’t speak to me. Fast forward 15 years. I was trekking in Nepal’s Annapurna range and found it on a hikers’ bookshelf. I reread it in my tent by candlelight. I couldn’t believe how great it was. Jo is amazing!

The book I reread

The Virgin Suicides by Jeffrey Eugenides. The writing is extraordinary, and the point of view is one of a kind. There isn’t a wasted word in the entire book. I also love to read essays and often return to The White Album by Joan Didion to study the way she crafts sentences. She has an amazing ability to capture the energy of an age, a movement, a fad, just as it begins to slide.

The book I could never read again

The Gormenghast Trilogy by Mervyn Peake. I loved this when I was a teenager and maybe I would love it again, but I don’t want to run the risk of spoiling my good memories.

The book I discovered later in life

So Long, See You Tomorrow by William Maxwell. It’s told from the point of view of a man in his 60s looking back on a childhood upended by murder and the loss of his mother. It’s a brilliant study of how impossible it is to make sense of our memories, because they have a bad habit of rewriting themselves.

The book I am currently reading

May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry.

My comfort read

Grimms’ Fairy Tales.

entries.title: Under Fire by Humza Yousaf – a deeply affecting story of being stranded in Gaza
entries.summary: The former Scottish first minister writes of his in-laws’ plight and the tragedy of those who weren’t so luckyA week into Israel’s bombing of Gaza in 2023, which followed Hamas’s deadly terrorist attack on Israel, Scotland’s then first minister Humza Yousaf received a text from his mother-in-law, Elizabeth. “Humza, I think we are about to die. entries.content:
A week into Israel’s bombing of Gaza in 2023, which followed Hamas’s deadly terrorist attack on Israel, Scotland’s then first minister Humza Yousaf received a text from his mother-in-law, Elizabeth. “Humza, I think we are about to die. I need you to promise me that you will take care of my girls.”

Elizabeth, a retired nurse from Dundee, and her Palestinian husband, Maged, had been visiting family in Gaza and become trapped there when the bombing began. Not only were people dying all around them, but their house was filling up with friends and neighbours whose homes had been destroyed, and they were running out of food. On the night Elizabeth texted, they had been told to leave their neighbourhood of Deir al-Balah ahead of a fresh wave of Israeli strikes. They later learned the evacuation order was a false alarm. Even so, Yousaf reflects, “in the four weeks from hell, this felt like the lowest point”.

Under Fire is a short yet deeply affecting book detailing Yousaf and his wife Nadia El-Nakla’s month-long nightmare as Elizabeth and Maged remained stranded in Gaza, during which they made repeated attempts to flee. The Israeli government had said it would let foreign nationals leave, though for Yousaf’s in-laws this appeared to be an empty pledge. More than once they made the perilous journey to Rafah, on the border with Egypt, only to be turned away when they got there. Meanwhile, Nadia’s brother was working in a Gaza hospital and sending desperate updates about civilian casualties, the lack of clean water and medical supplies and how he was performing surgeries without anaesthetic, often lit by the light from a mobile phone.

Yousaf and his family’s agonising plight unfolds as he goes about his duties as the newly elected first minister. The text from Elizabeth arrived during the SNP conference, on the eve of his first speech. As a result, much of the narrative concerns his efforts to meet his responsibilities in Scotland while trying to comfort and support his wife and children. All the while, he and his aides plead with the Foreign Office in London to help get Elizabeth and Maged out.

Yousaf is a natural communicator and, though his writing sometimes lacks flair, he effectively conveys the stress and torment that comes with attending meetings and delivering speeches while wrestling with what to make public and what to keep private regarding his family. In the end he decides to share what is happening to his in-laws to raise awareness about the horrors being visited on Gaza’s civilian population. The title Under Fire has a dual meaning, describing the terrifying ordeal of Palestinians in Gaza and the scrutiny and criticism that comes not just with being Scotland’s first minister but the first Muslim leader of a country that is 95% non-Muslim and overwhelmingly white.

There is another narrative here concerning Yousaf’s struggles to make his way politically and step out of the shadow of his mentor and predecessor Nicola Sturgeon, which sits awkwardly in a book that is primarily about a family in crisis. Similarly, his diatribe about Kate Forbes, his rival for the top job, and her “clumsy” leadership campaign would suit a straightforward political memoir, but here feels out of place.

More pertinent are Yousaf’s criticisms of the then British foreign secretary James Cleverly for initially failing to pick up the phone to him, even after he had spoken publicly about his parents-in-law being stranded. Neither does he mince his words about Rishi Sunak, whom he chastises for failing to provide updates for worried British citizens with family in Gaza.

entries.title: Children’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novels
entries.summary: A sumptuous collection of fairytales; a dreamy Minotaur retelling; the explosive finale of the YA Torch Trilogy and moreDogs, Dogs, Dogs by John Devolle, Pushkin, £12.99 “Old dogs, young dogs, dogs on wheels, dogs that want to eat your meals” – this “very silly book about dogs” is a polychromatic picture-book treat for little canine fans, full of bold graphic artwork and audacious rhymes.More! by
entries.content:
Dogs, Dogs, Dogs by John Devolle, Pushkin, £12.99

“Old dogs, young dogs, dogs on wheels, dogs that want to eat your meals” – this “very silly book about dogs” is a polychromatic picture-book treat for little canine fans, full of bold graphic artwork and audacious rhymes.

More! by Ged Adamson, Moon and Bird, £12.99

Best friends Squirrel and Mouse are on a blissful walk together, but Squirrel keeps wanting more – a hat, a tie, a boingy stick! – until he realises it’s all pointless without Mouse to share it. A slyly hilarious anti-consumerist picture book that encourages small readers to pore over its delightful background details.

The Tale That Time Sews by Sita Brahmachari, illustrated by Jane Ray, Templar, £12.99

A little girl waits for her new sibling to be born while Nana stitches together family stories in a quilt that will wrap them both in this 5+ picture book; a lyrical, beautiful account of displacement, migration and learning to flourish in new places while remembering your roots.

Little Minotaur by Gaia Alessi, Walker, £14.99

In ancient Crete, a boy with a bull head is cherished by his sister Ariadne and mother Pasiphaë. Though he struggles to form words, he rejoices in the natural world. But when fearful rumours rise up, he must find his place – and a better ending to his story – in this dreamy, beguiling picturebook Minotaur retelling for 5+.

Pomona: Stories of the Cat Witch by Tor Freeman, Guppy, £14.99

Pomona the cat witch lives in the forest, surrounded by pals including Ratso, Elfis and Prince Frog. It’s here that she discovers empathy while dusting her house, finds a friend for a lonely caterpillar and helps Ratso break an annoying curse. These daft, whimsical, highly illustrated stories are perfect for 5+ readers with a taste for thoughtful silliness.

A Year of Fairy Tales by Sophie Anderson, illustrated by Elisa Paganelli, Usborne, £25

This sumptuous hardback collection – one story for every month – features retellings of classic fairytales like Jack and the Beanstalk as well as original tales rooted in world folklore. Anderson’s lively, adventurous writing marries with Paganelli’s swirling, soaring artwork to create a treasure trove for 7+ readers to share at bedtime or explore solo.

Lumi and the Wolf by Lottie Saahko, Hachette, £14.99

Sent to stay with relatives in Lapland, autistic Lumi struggles to adapt, and her family warns her that a dangerous white wolf is lurking. When she befriends the wolf, Lumi and local boy Oskár set out on a perilous journey to the national park where Wolf can be safe – though she will have to use all her sharp senses and stored knowledge to get him there. Atmospheric and fast-paced, with intricately drawn illustrations, this tense, heartfelt 9+ animal adventure deals both with the impact of climate change on traditional Sami ways of life, and the deep human need to find where you belong.

The Rambler’s Curse by Mikey Please, HarperCollins, £14.99

Things are going well for the magical Café at the Edge of the Woods until a terrifying customer arrives: a human. His appearance sets off a chaotic chain reaction, involving a temperamental wizard’s staff, a red motorbike, a stolen gold hoard and a blanket of carnivorous moss. Can chef Rene and waiter Glumfoot defend the Woods from catastrophe in this laugh-out-loud, shaggy-dog spiral of purposes mistook? Developing the world and characters of Please’s Waterstones prize-winning picture book, this is the first in a trilogy for 8+.

Girl With a Sabretooth Tiger by Jasbinder Bilan, Chicken House, £7.99

In prehistoric England, 11-year-old Swallow, afraid her baby sister will die, undertakes a dangerous quest: to fetch a piece of green jadeite from the heart of a mountain god. Ishi, a village boy, insists on coming too – but it’s the spirit of the great tiger whose tooth she wears that will guide and protect her in this poetic, powerful, pared-back 9+ story of love, determination, courage and shared resource.

Anger Is Only a Shadow by Elizabeth Acevedo, Hot Key, £8.99

Lil is on probation. She needs to be New Lil – staying head down and out of trouble until her next court hearing – but Old Lil, barely contained, is desperate to make bad, impulsive decisions. Then her brother Aldwin, hundreds of miles away at college, starts talking about hearing voices, and Lil realises she’s the only one who can help. But can she get to him without sacrificing her freedom? A poignant, complex, thought-provoking YA novel by a Carnegie-winning author.

Nightcurse by Emma Hinds, Usborne, £9.99

Revenant Emrys Swift has been 17 for 157 years, living a cloistered life in a secret magical library and trying to remember his own death. When three important books go missing, he must collaborate with his nemesis, charismatic shapeshifter Aubrey Vale, to figure out where and why, but as spectral warnings rise around them, and the secrets of Emrys’s death and Aubrey’s life are laid bare, could their antipathy be changing to attraction? A gorgeously readable queer enemies-to-lovers romantasy, set in a richly realised magical world.

Flarestorm by Moira Buffini, Faber, £9.99

In a world where telepaths called Torches are either oppressed or exalted, an uprising is under way, seeking equality for all. The rebels are marching on the Capital, but Torches Elsa and Kaira are struggling to break out of their underground prison, while Rye, in captivity, is being forced to track powerful Torch Petra as she flies into the unknown. And where will conniving Zara Swan decide her ultimate loyalty lies? Messy, explosive, bloody and brutal, the concluding volume of the bestselling YA Torch Trilogy resolves multiple storylines and perspectives in a blaze of pain, fear, loss and glory.

entries.title: Helen Fielding launches Bridget Jones prize for northern comedy writing
entries.summary: The Yorkshire-born author says that the 1,000 word competition is for people ‘just living their lives being quietly hilarious’Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding has launched a comedy writing prize in the name of her most famous creation, aimed at unearthing funny new voices from the north of England.The Bridget Jones prize for northern comedy writing will go to the funniest self-contained, first-
entries.content:
Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding has launched a comedy writing prize in the name of her most famous creation, aimed at unearthing funny new voices from the north of England.

The Bridget Jones prize for northern comedy writing will go to the funniest self-contained, first-person prose of 1,000 words. The format echoes the anonymous diary columns in the Independent that first brought Bridget to readers in the mid-1990s.

Fielding, who grew up in Yorkshire, wrote the original columns and four Bridget Jones novels, as well as co-writing the blockbuster film adaptations starring Renée Zellweger.

She said Bridget’s humour was drawn from the people she grew up with: “laughing together at our mess-ups; bringing the fancy and pretentious down to earth”.

“There are lots of famous northern comics,” she said. “But this prize is for the comic voices of people who aren’t famous: just living their lives being quietly hilarious.”

Writers living in the north who have neither been published nor signed with an agent are eligible to enter. There is no entry fee and the winner will take home £2,000, plus a session with Aitken Alexander Associates, the agency that represents Fielding, and tailored support from the charity New Writing North. One runner-up will get £1,000.

Fielding was strict about the word limit. “I always tried to make the Bridget columns exactly 1,000 words long – like making the petrol pump stop at exactly 20 quid,” she said. “If it’s slightly under you won’t be punished. Just DON’T MAKE IT ANY LONGER!”

Fielding will judge alongside an Aitken Alexander agent and a representative from New Writing North, and the winner will be revealed at next summer’s Northern Writers’ awards in Newcastle, with the prize presented by Fielding. The prize will be given out each year until 2029.

Will Mackie from New Writing North said: “This is the first time the Northern Writers’ awards have featured an award exclusively for comedy writing.

“There is no one more fitting to identify an original comedy voice than Helen, who created one of the nation’s most beloved comic characters of the last 30 years.”

Fielding cited Victoria Wood, Alan Bennett, Les Dawson, Thora Hird and Morecambe and Wise as inspirations.

Submissions open on 23 November and close on 1 February 2027.

entries.title: Female Life on Planet Earth by Laleh Khadivi review – a mother’s secret past in the Iranian revolution
entries.summary: A woman living in California discovers her mother may have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic revolution, in an intriguing novel of inheritance and identity“It’s a little scary, isn’t it, inheritance?” That’s what Heti, the protagonist of Laleh Khadivi’s latest novel, remarks to a “soccer mom” as they watch their daughters play. “We don’t get to choose what we inherit. Or what we pass on.” H
entries.content:
“It’s a little scary, isn’t it, inheritance?” That’s what Heti, the protagonist of Laleh Khadivi’s latest novel, remarks to a “soccer mom” as they watch their daughters play. “We don’t get to choose what we inherit. Or what we pass on.” Heti, who lives in Los Angeles, is Iranian-American and works for an accountancy firm. She has two daughters, Ava and Zora, and her mother has recently died. When Ava scores a goal, the soccer mom asks, “Did she get that from you?”, but Heti is less interested in the skills that parents pass to their children than the secrets they keep from them.

Khadivi’s novel is about mothers and the mysteries they contain. In Female Life on Planet Earth she asks what happens when the people closest to us turn out to be strangers. How do we manage our grief and memorialise our loss when those we love have hidden awful parts of their lives? At the beginning of the book, Heti receives strict instructions from an Iranian aunt about the correct way to mark her mother’s passing. “One year after the death you throw a party,” she is told, “so that [people] can think about your mother, really remember and mourn her.” But then Heti receives a startling set of photographs from an unknown sender. In one image, a younger version of her mother stands veiled in black, a machine gun slung over her shoulder. In a second image, the weapon is extended towards a group of handcuffed women, “their miniskirts uneven on their hips, rips in their tight sweaters”, some crying before the camera, another lying prone, “face pressed into the concrete floor”.

Could her mother have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic Revolution in Iran? Khadivi doesn’t pose the question so bluntly. Instead, she allows the impact of the images to reverberate for Heti. The pictures with the gun are disturbing, but it is the “shock of affinity” that startles her most of all. “Even though I’m terrified by these pictures, I understand her urge to have control … For the tiniest second I was weirdly reassured that my mother wasn’t all manners and sweetness and that maybe we had more in common than I thought.”

Later, she visits her local library and reads about all-female militias, women who in “their newfound zeal … found the punishment of their sisters, the task assigned them by the revolutionaries, to be a satisfying outlet of power”. It’s a grimly fascinating history, but Khadivi is less interested in raking over the political complexities than in attending to the dissonance it stirs in Heti. She allows Heti to puzzle through her uncertain feelings in a novel that fluctuates in tone, serious and sardonic, analytical and droll by turns.

The drollery is partly an effect of the book’s structure – a series of vignettes dotted over the course of a year in which Heti wrestles with big issues in incongruous places. On the soccer pitch, she is bemused by the mom who complains, “You can’t believe all that Barbie feminist crap.” At the wholesale supermarket, with its “maze of open freezers filled with thirty pound turkeys”, she wonders if she is remembering her mother “as she really was or as I want her to be”. Doing the accounts on the set of a soft porn film, she decides that what “happens in these shoots is a kind of freedom … Where I came from, where my mother and I were born, a woman’s pleasure can destroy her.”

Standing in contrast to the comic parts of Heti’s suburban life is Khadivi’s more cosmic sensibility – suggested by the book’s title. Chapters are named for planets or taken from terms in physics, but the shift between the domestic and the metaphysical can make reading an uneven experience. Khadivi can be grandiose: “At night, Heti’s soul ranged and she followed. Without direction or orientation her thoughts spread into undefined time and limitless space.” At other times, the cosmos is an effective analogy: the “emotional gravity” of Heti’s experience pulls her “into a freefall” that feels like grasping at Jupiter’s vaporous atmosphere. In such circumstances, as Heti tells her daughters, “either you fall and fall or you figure out how to fly …”

When Zora later expresses her determination to act on the climate crisis, she tells her mother that “it’s going to be our job to do the extreme things, like take hostages, or destroy oil tankers, or stop eating meat just to get people to care. I’m ready to do any of those.” Khadivi positions Zora’s radicalism as an intriguing mirror to that of her grandmother, quietly challenging any easy assumptions a reader might have about the rights of one and the wrongs of another. If mothers can conceal their lives from their daughters, Khadivi is right to point to how daughters can carry forward, resist or remake the legacies they inherit. As Heti comes to understand in this intriguing and unusual novel, perhaps the more important question may be not what we inherit, but what we choose to become.

entries.title: Black Bag by Luke Kennard audiobook review – brilliant Booker-shortlisted campus comedy
entries.summary: The author reveals his mastery of comic timing in his narration of this novel about a cash-strapped actor paid to live inside a black leather bagThe unnamed narrator of Luke Kennard’s novel is an out-of-work actor living in London. His last job was three months ago, he is behind with his rent and has “measured out my life in coffees I cannot technically afford”. So when he comes across an advert –
entries.content:
The unnamed narrator of Luke Kennard’s novel is an out-of-work actor living in London. His last job was three months ago, he is behind with his rent and has “measured out my life in coffees I cannot technically afford”. So when he comes across an advert – “Male actor required for psychological enquiry. Non-speaking but discretion and devotion to restrictive performance requirements obligatory” – he offers his services.

The job, he discovers, is at a university working under a psychology professor named Dr Blend. There he must strip to his underpants and zip himself into a black leather bag, in which there are two eyeholes and further holes for his feet. The actor is expected to sit silently in the bag during seminars while students contemplate his presence.

The inspiration for Kennard’s Booker-shortlisted campus comedy is a 1967 social experiment, conducted at Oregon State University, where a student attended classes inside a black bag in a test to see whether other students would grow attached to his presence. It also nods to Yoko Ono’s 1964 conceptual artwork Bag Piece, in which gallery-goers were asked to climb inside a large black bag.

Kennard, who is the reader, mines this surreal conceit for laughs as the protagonist does battle with revolving doors and tries to pay for coffee using a card taped to the inside of the bag at chest height. As with his prose, the author’s delivery reveals him as a master of comic timing and a mordant bon mot. Yet beneath Black Bag’s winningly oddball exterior are more sober reflections on human relationships and what it is to be a man.

Available via John Murray, 9hr 12min

Further listening

Battle Axe: A Memoir

Margaret Hodge, William Collins, 14hr 43min

The veteran Labour politician narrates her book detailing 50 years in frontline politics, from her early career as a leader of Islington council to her time as an MP during the Tony Blair and Gordon Brown premierships and her recent work as the UK’s anti-corruption champion.

I Shoot Rock Stars

Tim Pope, Wildfire, 10hr 6min

Pope, a music video director, recalls wild moments with musicians of yore, from the time he dressed Freddie Mercury as a “giant Mediterranean prawn” to filming the Cure performing inside a wardrobe. Read by the author.
